1a.html:
Given: \Delta H = 2\ \mathrm{eV} per vacancy, T = 1000\ \mathrm{K}, u = 1.6 imes10^{-15}\ \mathrm{Hz} (normal atoms), u^{\prime} = 0.6 imes10^{-15}\ \mathrm{Hz} (beside a vacancy), z = 4, 1\ \mathrm{eV} = 1.6 imes10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}, k = 1.38 imes10^{-23}\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}.

Find: the equilibrium vacancy fraction and number.

Solution. Minimising the free energy (formation enthalpy against configurational entropy) gives

rac{n}{N} = \exp\left( rac{\Delta S_v}{k} ight)\exp\left(- rac{\Delta H}{kT} ight)

In the Einstein model each of the z neighbours of a vacancy has its three oscillators softened from u to u^{\prime}, so \Delta S_v = 3zk\ln( u/ u^{\prime}):

egin{aligned} rac{\Delta H}{kT} &= rac{3.2 imes10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}}{(1.38 imes10^{-23}\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}})(1000\ \mathrm{K})} = 23.19, \qquad e^{-23.19} = 8.50 imes10^{-11} \ \left( rac{ u}{ u^{\prime}} ight)^{3z} &= (2.667)^{12} = e^{11.77} = 1.29 imes10^{5} \ rac{n}{N} &= (1.29 imes10^{5})(8.50 imes10^{-11}) = 1.10 imes10^{-5} \end{aligned}

Per mole of sites: (6.022 imes10^{23})(1.10 imes10^{-5}) = 6.6 imes10^{18}. With the slide's molar volume of MgO, 11.3\ \mathrm{cm^3\,mol^{-1}}: 5.9 imes10^{17}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}.

Answer: n/N \approx 1.1 imes10^{-5}, about 6.6 imes10^{18} vacancies per mole (5.9 imes10^{17}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}).
pts: States n/N = \exp(\Delta S_v/k)\exp(-\Delta H/kT)
Vibrational entropy \Delta S_v = 3zk\ln( u/ u^{\prime}), pre-factor ( u/ u^{\prime})^{3z}
\Delta H/kT = 23.19 and \exp(-23.19) = 8.5\times10^{-11}, with eV converted to J
Entropy factor (1.6/0.6)^{12} = 1.29\times10^{5}
Final n/N \approx 1.1\times10^{-5}
Converts to a number: 6.6\times10^{18} per mole or about 6\times10^{17}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}
1a.src: Defects in ceramics: point defects and non-stoichiometry, slides 7, 10; Carter and Norton, Ceramic Materials, pp 200-201; Standard textbook treatment
1a.watch:
• The printed frequencies of 10^{-15} Hz are a slip (lattice vibrations are about 10^{13} Hz); only the ratio enters.
  • Softening only the one mode of each neighbour that points at the vacancy gives \Delta S_v = zk\ln(\nu/\nu^{\prime}) and 4.3\times10^{-9}; state the model you use.
  • Without the entropy term the answer would be 8.5\times10^{-11}: the softer vibrations raise it about 10^5 times.

1b.html:
(i) \mathrm{Nb_2O_5} dissolving in \mathrm{TiO_2}

\mathrm{Nb^{5+}} on a \mathrm{Ti^{4+}} site is the donor \mathrm{Nb_{Ti}^{\bullet}}. Two Nb fill two Ti sites, which take four O sites, so the fifth oxygen must go:

\mathrm{Nb_2O_5} \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{TiO_2}\ } 2\mathrm{Nb_{Ti}^{\bullet}} + 4\mathrm{O_O^{\times}} + \tfrac12\mathrm{O_2(g)} + 2e^{\prime}\quad(\text{low } p_{\mathrm{O_2}})
2\mathrm{Nb_2O_5} \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{TiO_2}\ } 4\mathrm{Nb_{Ti}^{\bullet}} + \mathrm{V_{Ti}^{\prime\prime\prime\prime}} + 10\mathrm{O_O^{\times}}\quad(\text{high } p_{\mathrm{O_2}})

Both keep Ti : O = 1 : 2 and balance charge (+2 - 2; +4 - 4). The first makes \mathrm{TiO_2} n-type.

(ii) Oxygen loss from \mathrm{MO_2}

Each oxygen leaves its site as \tfrac12\mathrm{O_2} and its two electrons stay behind, so the vacancy is fully ionised:

\mathrm{O_O^{\times}} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}} + 2e^{\prime} + \tfrac12\mathrm{O_2(g)}

For the whole reaction \mathrm{MO_2(s)} = \mathrm{MO_{2-x}} + \tfrac{x}{2}\mathrm{O_2(g)}:

\mathrm{M_M^{\times}} + 2\mathrm{O_O^{\times}} \rightarrow \mathrm{M_M^{\times}} + (2-x)\mathrm{O_O^{\times}} + x\,\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}} + 2x\,e^{\prime} + \tfrac{x}{2}\mathrm{O_2(g)}

With K = [\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}]\,n^2\,p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{1/2} and n = 2[\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}]: [\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}] = (K/4)^{1/3}p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{-1/6}.
pts: (i) Nb on a Ti site written as \mathrm{Nb_{Ti}^{\bullet}}

(i) A balanced reaction: electronic (2\mathrm{Nb_{Ti}^{\bullet}} + 4\mathrm{O_O^{\times}} + \tfrac12\mathrm{O_2} + 2e^{\prime}) or vacancy (4\mathrm{Nb_{Ti}^{\bullet}} + \mathrm{V_{Ti}^{\prime\prime\prime\prime}} + 10\mathrm{O_O^{\times}})
(i) Checks the 1:2 site ratio and charge, or gives the second compensation
(ii) \mathrm{O_O^{\times}} \to \mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}} + 2e^{\prime} + \tfrac12\mathrm{O_2}, balanced
(ii) Scales it to x for \mathrm{MO_2} \to \mathrm{MO_{2-x}} + \tfrac{x}{2}\mathrm{O_2}
(ii) Mass action with n = 2[\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}], giving p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{-1/6}
1b.src: Defects in ceramics: point defects and non-stoichiometry, slides 6, 12, 20-21; Carter and Norton, Ceramic Materials, p 203
1b.watch:
• "Fully ionised" means the double dot on the vacancy and two free electrons; \mathrm{V_O^{\times}} or \mathrm{V_O^{\bullet}} are the partly ionised steps.
  • In \mathrm{TiO_{2-x}} the electrons localise as \mathrm{Ti^{3+}} (\mathrm{Ti_{Ti}^{\prime}}), but they are still written e^{\prime} in the reaction.

1c.html:
In tape casting a doctor blade spreads a slurry on a moving carrier film; it dries to a flexible green tape that is cut, laminated, debinded and sintered. A better film is uniform, dense, smooth and free of cracks, pores and warping:

  1. Powder: fine (below 1\ \mu\mathrm{m}), narrow-sized, unagglomerated and pure (slide 15), so packing and shrinkage are uniform.
  2. Slurry (Carter Table 27.1): solvent for viscosity; dispersant (fish oil, steric) against settling; binder (PVB) for green strength; plasticisers for flexibility. Mill powder, dispersant and solvent first, then add binder and plasticiser. Use high solids, then de-air and filter.
  3. Rheology: shear-thinning slurry that flows under the blade and sets at once, so the tape does not spread.
  4. Casting: blade gap h, speed, slurry head and viscosity set the thickness; keep them constant (a double blade evens the head) on a flat carrier, and monitor thickness on line.
  5. Drying: slow, with counter-current air and a solvent-rich start, against skinning, cracks and curling; thickness roughly halves (1.50 to 0.75 mm, Carter).
  6. Burnout and sintering: slow heating through binder burnout against blisters; sinter flat against warping (0.75 to 0.60 mm).
pts: Outlines the process: slurry, doctor blade, moving carrier, drying, green tape, sintering
Fine, narrow-sized, unagglomerated, pure powder for uniform packing and shrinkage
Slurry formulation: solvent, dispersant, binder, plasticiser, with their roles; two-stage milling; high solids
De-airing and filtering the slurry; shear-thinning rheology
Thickness control: blade gap, speed, slurry head, viscosity; uniform carrier; on-line thickness check
Controlled slow drying (counter-current air, solvent-rich start) against cracks and curling; large drying shrinkage
Slow binder burnout and flat sintering against blisters and warping
Draws the tape caster with labels
1c.sketch: • Reservoir, doctor blade and gap h, moving carrier, drying zone with counter-flow air, green tape.
1c.src: Sintering, colloid chemistry and sol-gel, slides 15, 19-20, 41; Carter and Norton, Ceramic Materials, pp 494-496; Standard textbook treatment
1c.watch:
• Too much binder and plasticiser lowers the green density and raises sintering shrinkage; too little makes the tape crack on handling.
  • Carter's trichloroethylene-ethanol solvent is toxic; water-based slurries (with polyelectrolyte dispersants and acrylic binders) are now common but dry more slowly and crack more easily.

2a.fix: Slide 6 of the dielectric ceramics deck lists strontium titanate with a relative dielectric constant of 100,000. Bulk \mathrm{SrTiO_3} at room temperature has \varepsilon_r of about 300: it is paraelectric with \theta_c near 0 K and a Curie constant of 7.0\times10^{4} K, which by the Curie-Weiss law gives about 230 at 300 K; measured values are about 300. Effective values of 10^{4} to 10^{5} belong to grain-boundary barrier-layer capacitors of semiconducting \mathrm{SrTiO_3}, where the high value comes from interfacial (space-charge) polarisation, not from the crystal itself. Do not use 100,000 as the dielectric constant of \mathrm{SrTiO_3}.
2a.html:
The dielectric constant measures how much a material polarises, \varepsilon_r = 1 + P/\varepsilon_0E, with P = \sum N_j\alpha_jE. It therefore depends on which polarisation mechanisms a material has, and how strong each is:

  • Electronic only (covalent or non-polar solids): small, \varepsilon_r \approx n^2. Polyethylene 2.3, diamond 5.7.
  • Electronic plus ionic (ionic ceramics): moderate. The ionic term is limited by bond stiffness, \alpha_i = q^2/Yd_0. NaCl 5.9, \mathrm{Al_2O_3} about 9.
  • Permanent dipoles add a large orientation term: water about 80.
  • Coupled, switchable dipoles (ferroelectrics): very large. In \mathrm{BaTiO_3} the off-centre \mathrm{Ti^{4+}} gives \kappa \approx 1600 to 5000, about 10^{4} at its Curie point.

Example 1, \mathrm{Al_2O_3}: stiff ionic bonds and no permanent dipoles give \kappa \approx 9, a good insulator.

Example 2, \mathrm{BaTiO_3}: permanent dipoles in domains give \kappa in the thousands, a few hundred times larger: a capacitor dielectric.

Frequency, temperature and impurities (space charge) shift the values further, so \kappa spans about 2 to 10^{4}.
pts: Explains that \varepsilon_r depends on the polarisation mechanisms present and their polarisability, P = \sum N\alpha E
Electronic only gives small values (\varepsilon_r \approx n^2, about 2 to 12); electronic plus ionic gives moderate values (about 5 to 10 in most ceramics)
Permanent or coupled dipoles (dipolar, ferroelectric) give very large values
Example 1 with its value and mechanism, such as \mathrm{Al_2O_3} about 9 (electronic plus ionic)
Example 2 with its value and mechanism, such as \mathrm{BaTiO_3} 1600 to 5000 (off-centre \mathrm{Ti^{4+}}, ferroelectric domains)
Notes that frequency, temperature or impurities also change \varepsilon_r
2a.src: Dielectric ceramics, slides 6, 8; Dielectrics class note (2024 scan), pp 10, 13, 17-18; Carter and Norton, Ceramic Materials, pp 570, 573
2a.watch:
• Choose two examples from different mechanism groups; two linear ceramics (say MgO and \mathrm{Al_2O_3}) do not show the "wide range".
  • Quote values with the frequency they apply to where you can: slide 8 gives \mathrm{Al_2O_3} 9.0 at 60 Hz but 6.5 at 1 MHz.

2b.html:
Given: stoichiometric \mathrm{M_2O_3}, E_g = 5\ \mathrm{eV}, \Delta H_F = 2\ \mathrm{eV}, \Delta H_S = 7\ \mathrm{eV}, D_{\mathrm{M,int}} = 1.42\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{cm^2\,s^{-1}} at T = 1000\ \mathrm{K}, \mu_h = 2000 and \mu_e = 8000\ \mathrm{cm^2\,V^{-1}\,s^{-1}}, N_c = N_v = 10^{22}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}, interstitial sites = 2\times cation sites, M = 40\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}, \rho = 4\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}.

Find: \sigma_{\mathrm{electronic}} and \sigma_{\mathrm{ionic}} at 1000 K, and the type of conductor.

Step 1, electronic carriers. Intrinsic excitation, \mathrm{null} \rightleftharpoons e^{\prime} + h^{\bullet}, with n = p in a stoichiometric oxide:

\begin{aligned} kT &= (8.617\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV\,K^{-1}})(1000\ \mathrm{K}) = 0.0862\ \mathrm{eV} \\ n = p &= (N_cN_v)^{1/2}\exp\left(-\frac{E_g}{2kT}\right) = 10^{22}\,e^{-29.01} = 2.5\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}} \\ \sigma_e &= ne(\mu_e + \mu_h) = (2.5\times10^{9})(1.6\times10^{-19})(10^{4}) = 4.0\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{S\,cm^{-1}} \end{aligned}

Step 2, ionic defects. \Delta H_F = 2\ \mathrm{eV} \ll \Delta H_S = 7\ \mathrm{eV}, so cation Frenkel pairs dominate: \mathrm{M_M^{\times}} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{M_i^{\bullet\bullet\bullet}} + \mathrm{V_M^{\prime\prime\prime}}.

\begin{aligned} N_f &= \frac{\rho N_A}{M} = \frac{(4)(6.022\times10^{23})}{40} = 6.02\times10^{22}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}, \quad N = 2N_f = 1.20\times10^{23}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}},\ N_i = 2N \\ [\mathrm{M_i^{\bullet\bullet\bullet}}] &= (NN_i)^{1/2}\exp\left(-\frac{\Delta H_F}{2kT}\right) = (1.70\times10^{23})\,e^{-11.60} = 1.55\times10^{18}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}} \end{aligned}

The vacancies made with them are immobile, as the question states, so only \mathrm{M_i^{\bullet\bullet\bullet}} carries ionic current.

Step 3, ionic mobility (Nernst-Einstein), z = 3.

\begin{aligned} \mu_i &= \frac{zeD}{kT} = \frac{3\,(1.42\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{cm^2\,s^{-1}})}{0.0862\ \mathrm{V}} = 4.9\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{cm^2\,V^{-1}\,s^{-1}} \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{ion}} &= [\mathrm{M_i^{\bullet\bullet\bullet}}]\,ze\,\mu_i = (1.55\times10^{18})(3)(1.6\times10^{-19})(4.9\times10^{-9}) = 3.7\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{S\,cm^{-1}} \end{aligned}

Step 4, compare. \sigma_e/\sigma_{\mathrm{ion}} \approx 1.1\times10^{3}, so the ionic transference number is t_{\mathrm{ion}} \approx 0.001.

Answer: at 1000 K the oxide is an electronic conductor: \sigma_e \approx 4\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{S\,cm^{-1}} against \sigma_{\mathrm{ion}} \approx 4\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{S\,cm^{-1}}. Although there are 10^{9} times more interstitials than free electrons, the electronic mobilities are about 10^{12} times larger.
pts: (electronic) n = p = (N_cN_v)^{1/2}\exp(-E_g/2kT) \approx 2.5\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}
(electronic) \sigma_e = ne(\mu_e + \mu_h) \approx 4.0\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{S\,cm^{-1}}
Chooses cation Frenkel disorder because 2\ \mathrm{eV} \ll 7\ \mathrm{eV}, writing \mathrm{M_i^{\bullet\bullet\bullet}} + \mathrm{V_M^{\prime\prime\prime}}
Site densities from \rho N_A/M: N = 1.20\times10^{23} cation sites per \mathrm{cm^3}, N_i = 2N
[\mathrm{M_i^{\bullet\bullet\bullet}}] = (NN_i)^{1/2}\exp(-\Delta H_F/2kT) \approx 1.6\times10^{18}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}
Nernst-Einstein mobility \mu_i = zeD/kT \approx 4.9\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{cm^2\,V^{-1}\,s^{-1}} with z = 3
\sigma_{\mathrm{ion}} \approx 3.7\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{S\,cm^{-1}}
Concludes electronic conductor, \sigma_e/\sigma_{\mathrm{ion}} \approx 10^{3} (t_{\mathrm{ion}} \approx 0.001)
2b.src: Defects in ceramics: point defects and non-stoichiometry, slides 9, 11-13; Carter and Norton, Ceramic Materials, pp 200-203; Standard textbook treatment
2b.watch:
• The Frenkel enthalpy is per pair, so the exponent is \Delta H_F/2kT; using \Delta H_F/kT lowers \sigma_{\mathrm{ion}} another 10^{5} times.
  • "Twice the number of atomic sites" is read here as twice the cation sites. Counting all five atoms per formula unit gives [\mathrm{M_i}] = 2.5\times10^{18}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}} and \sigma_{\mathrm{ion}} = 5.8\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{S\,cm^{-1}}: the conclusion holds.
  • Schottky disorder in \mathrm{M_2O_3} forms five vacancies, so each fraction scales as \exp(-\Delta H_S/5kT) \approx 9\times10^{-8}, about 100 times below the Frenkel factor.
  • Confidence is medium only because the site wording is ambiguous; the printed molar mass (40 g/mol) is small for an \mathrm{M_2O_3}, but use it as given.

2c.html:
In a non-stoichiometric oxide the gas exchanges oxygen with the crystal, and every exchanged oxygen creates ionic defects plus electronic carriers. The mass-action law makes the carrier density a power of p_{\mathrm{O_2}}, so \log\sigma against \log p_{\mathrm{O_2}} is a straight line whose slope sign gives the carrier type.

Metal-deficient oxides (\mathrm{Fe_{1-x}O}, \mathrm{Ni_{1-x}O}, CoO): p-type.

\tfrac12\mathrm{O_2(g)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{O_O^{\times}} + \mathrm{V_M^{\prime\prime}} + 2h^{\bullet}, \qquad K = [\mathrm{V_M^{\prime\prime}}]\,p^2\,p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{-1/2}

With p = 2[\mathrm{V_M^{\prime\prime}}]: p = (2K)^{1/3}p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{+1/6}, so \sigma = pe\mu_h rises as p_{\mathrm{O_2}} rises (holes hop between \mathrm{Fe^{2+}} and \mathrm{Fe^{3+}}).

Oxygen-deficient oxides (\mathrm{TiO_{2-x}}, \mathrm{CeO_{2-x}}): n-type.

\mathrm{O_O^{\times}} \rightleftharpoons \tfrac12\mathrm{O_2(g)} + \mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}} + 2e^{\prime}, \qquad K = [\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}]\,n^2\,p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{1/2}

With n = 2[\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}]: n = (2K)^{1/3}p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{-1/6}, so \sigma rises on reduction. Metal-excess \mathrm{Zn_{1+x}O} (\mathrm{Zn_i^{\bullet}} + e^{\prime}) gives -1/4.

Real oxides combine the branches: undoped \mathrm{SrTiO_3} falls with slope -1/6 to -1/4, passes a minimum, then rises with +1/4. CaO-doped \mathrm{ZrO_2} has a flat ionic plateau where the dopant fixes [\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}].
pts: States that p_{\mathrm{O_2}} changes the oxygen content, which creates ionic defects plus electrons or holes, so \sigma \propto p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{\pm 1/m}

Metal-deficient reaction \tfrac12\mathrm{O_2} \to \mathrm{O_O^{\times}} + \mathrm{V_M^{\prime\prime}} + 2h^{\bullet} with mass action and p = 2[\mathrm{V_M^{\prime\prime}}], giving \sigma \propto p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{+1/6}

Oxygen-deficient reaction \mathrm{O_O^{\times}} \to \tfrac12\mathrm{O_2} + \mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}} + 2e^{\prime} with n = 2[\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}], giving \sigma \propto p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{-1/6}
Names examples of each type (\mathrm{Fe_{1-x}O}, NiO, CoO; \mathrm{TiO_{2-x}}, \mathrm{CeO_{2-x}}, ZnO)
Draws \log\sigma against \log p_{\mathrm{O_2}} with the +1/6 and -1/6 lines labelled
Notes a real oxide can show both branches with a minimum (\mathrm{SrTiO_3}), or an ionic plateau (CaO-\mathrm{ZrO_2})
2c.sketch:
• Axes \log\sigma against \log p_{\mathrm{O_2}}.
  • p-type \mathrm{M_{1-x}O} line of slope +1/6; n-type \mathrm{MO_{2-x}} line of slope -1/6 (or -1/4 for \mathrm{Zn_i^{\bullet}}).
  • A flat ionic line for a dopant-controlled electrolyte; mark the reducing direction.
2c.src: Defects in ceramics: point defects and non-stoichiometry, slides 18-20, 27-28, 30; Carter and Norton, Ceramic Materials, pp 203-204
2c.watch:
• The slope depends on the defect charge: singly ionised \mathrm{V_O^{\bullet}} or \mathrm{Zn_i^{\bullet}} give -1/4, neutral defects give no carriers. Measuring the slope is how the deck identifies \mathrm{Zn_i^{\bullet}} in ZnO.
  • Only oxides whose cation can change valence (Fe, Co, Ni, Ti, Ce) become non-stoichiometric; MgO and \mathrm{Al_2O_3} barely respond.

3a.html:
Ionic moments. \mathrm{Zn^{2+}} (Z = 30): [\mathrm{Ar}]3d^{10}, 0\,\mu_B. \mathrm{Cu^{2+}} (Z = 29): [\mathrm{Ar}]3d^9, 1 unpaired, 1\,\mu_B. \mathrm{Fe^{3+}} (Z = 26): [\mathrm{Ar}]3d^5, 5\,\mu_B.

Distribution. \mathrm{CuFe_2O_4} is inverse; \mathrm{Zn^{2+}} has the strongest A-site preference of all cations, so it displaces \mathrm{Fe^{3+}} from A to B:

(\mathrm{Zn}_x\mathrm{Fe}_{1-x})_A[\mathrm{Cu}_{1-x}\mathrm{Fe}_{1+x}]_B\mathrm{O_4}

Theoretical moment. A and B are antiparallel (strong A-O-B superexchange):

\begin{aligned} M_A &= 5(1-x), \qquad M_B = 1(1-x) + 5(1+x) = 6 + 4x \\ n_B &= M_B - M_A = 1 + 9x\ \ \mu_B\ \text{per formula unit} \end{aligned}
x00.20.40.60.81.0
n_B (\mu_B)1.02.84.66.48.210.0

So non-magnetic Zn raises the theoretical moment by 1.8\,\mu_B per 0.2 of Zn: it removes \mathrm{Fe^{3+}} moment from the opposing A sublattice and adds it to B.

Experimental fall near x of 0.5 (Yafet-Kittel).

  1. The A-B coupling (125^\circ bonds) is strong; the B-B coupling (90^\circ) is weak; both are antiferromagnetic.
  2. Zn dilutes the A sublattice, so the A-B molecular field acting on each B ion falls roughly as (1-x).
  3. Near x \approx 0.5 the B-B interaction can compete. The B sublattice splits into two halves canted by \pm\alpha_{YK} from the direction antiparallel to A, and
n_B = M_B\cos\alpha_{YK} - M_A
  1. \alpha_{YK} grows with x; in the molecular-field model \cos\alpha_{YK} = \lambda_{AB}M_A/(\lambda_{BB}M_B), so the canted moment, M_A(\lambda_{AB}/\lambda_{BB} - 1), falls with M_A. At x = 1, \alpha_{YK} = 90^\circ and n_B \to 0: \mathrm{ZnFe_2O_4} is antiferromagnetic (Neel temperature about 10 K).

The reduced Curie temperature of the diluted ferrite lowers room-temperature values further.
pts: Moments from Z: \mathrm{Zn^{2+}} 3d^{10} 0, \mathrm{Cu^{2+}} 3d^9 1\,\mu_B, \mathrm{Fe^{3+}} 3d^5 5\,\mu_B
Zn on A, Fe pushed to B: (\mathrm{Zn}_x\mathrm{Fe}_{1-x})_A[\mathrm{Cu}_{1-x}\mathrm{Fe}_{1+x}]_B\mathrm{O_4}
n_B = M_B - M_A = (6 + 4x) - 5(1-x) = 1 + 9x
Values 1.0, 2.8, 4.6, 6.4, 8.2, 10.0 \mu_B, showing the gradual increase
Dilution of A weakens the A-B coupling so the weak B-B antiferromagnetic coupling competes near x \approx 0.5
Yafet-Kittel canting of two B halves by \pm\alpha_{YK}, sketched
n_B = M_B\cos\alpha_{YK} - M_A, \alpha_{YK} rising to 90^\circ so n_B \to 0 for \mathrm{ZnFe_2O_4}
Molecular-field result \cos\alpha_{YK} = \lambda_{AB}M_A/(\lambda_{BB}M_B), or the lower Curie temperature with Zn
3a.sketch:
• n_B (\mu_B) against x: Neel line from 1 at x = 0 to 10 at x = 1; measured curve following it to x \approx 0.4, peaking, then falling towards 0.
  • Spin picture: A up; B_1 and B_2 down, tilted by \pm\alpha_{YK}.
3a.src: Lecture 03 Magnetic ceramics, slides 29, 36-41; Superexchange, pp 5-9; O'Handley, Modern Magnetic Materials, p 162; Standard textbook treatment
3a.watch:
• \mathrm{Cu^{2+}} is 3d^9 (1\,\mu_B), not 3d^{10}; do not confuse it with \mathrm{Cu^{+}}.
  • The measured \mathrm{CuFe_2O_4} moment is about 1.3\,\mu_B (orbital contribution and some Cu on A), which is why the slide's Cu curve starts above 1.
  • Apply \cos\alpha_{YK} to the B sublattice only.

3b.html:
Given: r_{\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}} = 0.74 Å, r_{\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}} = 0.745 Å, r_{\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}} = 0.645 Å, R_O = 1.42 Å; (i) x = 0.1; (ii) x = 0.9 with \alpha_{Y\text{-}K} = 80^\circ.

Find: the saturation moment n_B (\mu_B per formula unit) and the lattice parameter a of \mathrm{Zn_xCu_{1-x}Fe_2O_4}.

Solution

Step 1, distribution and ionic moments. \mathrm{CuFe_2O_4} is inverse and \mathrm{Zn^{2+}} goes to A:

(\mathrm{Zn}_x\mathrm{Fe}_{1-x})_A[\mathrm{Cu}_{1-x}\mathrm{Fe}_{1+x}]_B\mathrm{O_4}

Spin-only moments: \mathrm{Fe^{3+}} (3d^5) 5\,\mu_B, \mathrm{Cu^{2+}} (3d^9) 1\,\mu_B, \mathrm{Zn^{2+}} (3d^{10}) 0.

Step 2, sublattices. The strongest exchange is the antiferromagnetic A-O-B superexchange, so A moments are parallel to each other and antiparallel to B. Zn has no moment, so it lowers M_A and, by pushing \mathrm{Fe^{3+}} to B, raises M_B:

M_A = 5(1-x), \qquad M_B = 1(1-x) + 5(1+x)

At high Zn content the weakened A-B coupling lets the B-B antiferromagnetic exchange cant the two halves of the B sublattice by \alpha_{YK} (Yafet-Kittel), and only their component along the B axis counts:

n_B = M_B\cos\alpha_{YK} - M_A

with \alpha_{YK} = 0 for the collinear Neel arrangement at low Zn.

Step 3, lattice parameter:

a = \frac{8}{3\sqrt{3}}\left[(r_A + R_O) + \sqrt{3}\,(r_B + R_O)\right], \quad r_A = x r_{\mathrm{Zn}} + (1-x) r_{\mathrm{Fe}}, \quad r_B = \tfrac{1}{2}\left[(1-x) r_{\mathrm{Cu}} + (1+x) r_{\mathrm{Fe}}\right]

(i) x = 0.1 (collinear)

\begin{aligned} M_A &= 4.5\,\mu_B, \qquad M_B = 0.9 + 5.5 = 6.4\,\mu_B, \qquad n_B = 6.4 - 4.5 = 1.9\,\mu_B \\ r_A &= 0.1(0.74) + 0.9(0.645) = 0.6545\ \mathring{\mathrm{A}}, \qquad r_B = \tfrac{1}{2}\left[0.9(0.745) + 1.1(0.645)\right] = 0.690\ \mathring{\mathrm{A}} \\ a &= 1.5396\left[2.0745 + 1.7321(2.110)\right] = 8.821\ \mathring{\mathrm{A}} \end{aligned}

(ii) x = 0.9, alpha_YK = 80 degrees

\begin{aligned} M_A &= 5(0.1) = 0.5\,\mu_B, \qquad M_B = 0.1 + 5(1.9) = 9.6\,\mu_B \\ n_B &= 9.6\cos 80^\circ - 0.5 = 1.667 - 0.5 = 1.17\,\mu_B \quad (\text{Neel: } 9.1\,\mu_B) \\ r_A &= 0.9(0.74) + 0.1(0.645) = 0.7305\ \mathring{\mathrm{A}}, \qquad r_B = \tfrac{1}{2}\left[0.1(0.745) + 1.9(0.645)\right] = 0.650\ \mathring{\mathrm{A}} \\ a &= 1.5396\left[2.1505 + 1.7321(2.070)\right] = 8.831\ \mathring{\mathrm{A}} \end{aligned}

Answer: (i) n_B = 1.9\,\mu_B per formula unit, a = 8.82 Å; (ii) n_B = 1.17\,\mu_B per formula unit, a = 8.83 Å. With 8 formula units per cell, M_s = 8n_B\mu_B/a^3 \approx 205 and 126 kA/m. The cell hardly changes since r_{\mathrm{Zn}} \approx r_{\mathrm{Cu}} as printed; at x = 0.9 the canted B sublattice cuts the moment to about an eighth of the Neel value.

4b.fix: The printed question names \mathrm{LaTiO_3}. That is a centrosymmetric orthorhombic perovskite (a \mathrm{Ti^{3+}} Mott insulator) and cannot be pyroelectric. The pyroelectric on 435-diel slide 9 and in Carter is \mathrm{LiTaO_3}, lithium tantalate; the answer is written for it. The applications asked for are those of any pyroelectric, so an answer that keeps the printed name earns the same marks; one line noting the likely misprint is enough.
4b.html:
The materials. \mathrm{SiO_2} means crystalline \alpha-quartz: non-centrosymmetric, so piezoelectric, but non-polar, so not pyroelectric. The pyroelectric is taken as \mathrm{LiTaO_3} (slide 9); \mathrm{LaTiO_3} is centrosymmetric.

Piezoelectric quartz (D = dT + \varepsilon E, d \approx 2.3\ \mathrm{pC\,N^{-1}}; low loss, stable resonance):

  1. Crystal oscillators and filters. A plate driven by an AC voltage locks to its mechanical resonance, f = v/2t: the clock of watches, computers, phones and radios.
  2. Pressure and force sensors (charge Q = dF), accelerometers and microbalances.

Pyroelectric \mathrm{LiTaO_3} (P_s falls on warming, so i = pA\,dT/dt with p \approx 230\ \mu\mathrm{C\,m^{-2}\,K^{-1}}):

  1. Infrared detectors: passive infrared intruder alarms, flame and fire detectors.
  2. Thermal imaging cameras and laser power meters.
pts: Identifies \mathrm{SiO_2} as crystalline \alpha-quartz, piezoelectric (non-centrosymmetric) but not pyroelectric (non-polar)
Quartz application 1: crystal oscillator, resonator or filter, locked to the plate's mechanical resonance (watches, phones)
Quartz application 2: pressure or force sensor, accelerometer, microbalance or transducer, using Q = dF
Pyroelectric (\mathrm{LiTaO_3}) application 1: infrared detector (intruder alarm, fire detector), working by i = pA\,dT/dt
Pyroelectric (\mathrm{LiTaO_3}) application 2: thermal imaging camera, laser power meter or radiometer

4b.watch:
• Fused silica is not piezoelectric; only single-crystal \alpha-quartz is used, and it cannot be poled because it is not ferroelectric.
  • Quartz is not pyroelectric, so IR detection is not a quartz application.
  • A pyroelectric senses only a change in temperature: the IR is chopped, or the target must move.

4c.html:
The statement is justified. \mathrm{BaTiO_3} was the first ceramic found to be ferroelectric (1940s), raised available \kappa by about two orders of magnitude, and is still the basic capacitor dielectric. The cause is structural: large \mathrm{Ba^{2+}} expands the oxygen octahedron, so the small \mathrm{Ti^{4+}} (r_{\mathrm{Ti}}/r_{\mathrm{O}} = 0.44) rattles and, below \theta_c = 120^\circ\mathrm{C}, sits off-centre: every cell carries a dipole.

Properties and the uses they earn

  1. Very high \kappa: 1500 to 5000 at room temperature, about 10^{4} at \theta_c, with \tan\delta \le 0.025 and resistivity 10^{8} to 10^{15}\ \Omega\,\mathrm{cm}. Multilayer and disc capacitors need about a thousand times less plate area than polymer or vacuum ones; \mathrm{(Ba,Sr)TiO_3} films are high-\kappa DRAM capacitor dielectrics.
  2. Ferroelectric hysteresis at room temperature (P_s \approx 0.27\ \mathrm{C\,m^{-2}}, E_c \approx 0.1\ \mathrm{MV\,m^{-1}} in a crystal): switchable remanence for ferroelectric memories.
  3. Piezoelectric and pyroelectric after poling (d \approx 100 to 149 pC/N): transducers, sonar, pickups, IR sensors.
  4. Semiconducting when donor-doped: PTC thermistors, whose resistance jumps at \theta_c.
  5. Durable, lead-free, simple to make as ceramic, crystal or film, and tunable by solid solution and grain size.

Limitations

  • The \kappa peak is narrow and far from room temperature, so pure \mathrm{BaTiO_3} is little used: shifters (Sr, Zr), depressors and fine grains give the X7R and Z5U grades.
  • \kappa varies with temperature, DC bias and age, and its loss exceeds that of linear dielectrics.
  • Its low \theta_c limits piezoelectric use; PZT (d 250 to 365 pC/N) dominates transducers.

Conclusion. \mathrm{BaTiO_3} deserves its attention as the prototype ferroelectric and leading capacitor material, but it is used modified, not pure.
pts: Explains the origin: large \mathrm{Ba^{2+}}, small rattling \mathrm{Ti^{4+}} off-centre below \theta_c = 120^\circ\mathrm{C}, so a permanent dipole in every cell
High \kappa (1500 to 5000, about 10^{4} at \theta_c) with low loss and high resistivity, used in multilayer and disc capacitors
Ferroelectric hysteresis at room temperature (P_s, P_r, E_c), used in memories
Piezoelectric and pyroelectric after poling, used in transducers and IR sensors
Donor-doped semiconducting \mathrm{BaTiO_3} for PTC thermistors, or easy processing and lead-free composition
Gives the other side: narrow \kappa peak far from room temperature, needing shifters, depressors or fine grains (X7R, Z5U); or dependence on bias and ageing
Notes that PZT outperforms it as a piezoelectric
Sketches \varepsilon_r against T with the 120 °C peak, or a labelled P-E loop
Concludes that the statement holds but the material is used modified

• \varepsilon_r against T for \mathrm{BaTiO_3}: the sharp peak at 120 °C, Curie-Weiss fall above it, room temperature far below the peak.
  • A P-E loop with P_s, P_r and E_c labelled.

4c.watch:
• "Discuss" needs both sides and a conclusion; a list of applications alone loses the limitation marks.
  • Slide 8's \tan\delta of 0.0001 for \mathrm{BaTiO_3} is unusually low: the class note gives 0.015, and Carter's X7R grades allow up to 0.025. Quote a range.
  • The PTC jump comes from grain-boundary barriers that rise sharply when \kappa falls above \theta_c; give it only as a named use unless asked.

5a.html:
Transformation toughening needs metastable tetragonal (t) zirconia that turns monoclinic (m) under the crack-tip stress. The change is martensitic with about 4 to 5 % volume expansion, which compresses the crack tip (slides 13-14). Neither material has such a phase.

  • Pure \mathrm{ZrO_2}: sintered in the t field, it transforms to m by itself on cooling (near 950^\circ\mathrm{C}). The uncontrolled expansion cracks the part, and at room temperature it is already stable m, so nothing is left to transform at a crack.
  • Fully stabilised zirconia (about 8 mol% \mathrm{Y_2O_3} or more): cubic is stable down to room temperature and does not transform under stress, so K_{IC} stays about 3\ \mathrm{MPa\,m^{1/2}}.

Only partial stabilisation (3 to 8 mol% \mathrm{Y_2O_3}, slide 15) retains transformable t.
pts: Toughening requires metastable t that transforms to m (a few percent expansion) at the crack tip and compresses it
Pure zirconia turns to m spontaneously on cooling; the expansion cracks it and no t remains at room temperature
FSZ is cubic down to room temperature with no stress-induced transformation, so K_{IC} stays about 3\ \mathrm{MPa\,m^{1/2}}
5a.src: Mechanical properties, slides 13-15; Carter and Norton, Ceramic Materials, pp 344, 351-352
5a.watch: • Yttria itself does not toughen (slide 15); it only decides whether t survives. Too much gives FSZ, too little gives pure-zirconia behaviour.

6a.html:
Why statistics. A ceramic breaks at its most severe flaw (weakest link). Flaws vary randomly in size, position and orientation, so nominally identical specimens fail at different stresses (slide 10). One strength value with a safety factor (deterministic design) therefore fails; strength must be given as a probability.

Weibull distribution (slide 11).

P_f = 1 - \exp\left[-\frac{V}{V_0}\left(\frac{\sigma}{\sigma_0}\right)^m\right]

\sigma_0 is the characteristic strength (P_f = 0.632 at V = V_0) and m the Weibull modulus.

What m measures. m is the slope of \ln\ln(1/P_s) against \ln\sigma, found by ranking at least 30 results with P_f = j/(N + 1) (part b does this for nine bars). High m means a narrow strength band and a predictable, reliable material; low m means wide scatter. Ceramics have m \approx 5 to 20, steels about 100.

Use in design. The allowable stress for an accepted failure probability is

\sigma = \sigma_0\left[\ln\frac{1}{1 - P_f}\right]^{1/m}

For 1 failure in 1000 this is 0.25\sigma_0 at m = 5 but 0.71\sigma_0 at m = 20. Strength also falls with size, \sigma \propto V^{-1/m}: ten times the volume is 37 % weaker at m = 5, 11 % at m = 20. Hence bend strengths exceed tensile ones (slide 9).

Limits. One flaw population, test conditions matching service, and no slow crack growth are assumed; proof testing and stress-probability-time diagrams cover these.
pts: Strength is statistical: weakest-link failure from randomly distributed flaws gives scatter, so deterministic design fails
Weibull equation with \sigma_0 (P_f = 0.632) and m defined
m is the slope of \ln\ln(1/P_s) against \ln\sigma from ranked tests (about 30 or more)
High m = narrow distribution = reliable; ceramics 5 to 20 against about 100 for steels
Design use: \sigma = \sigma_0[\ln(1/(1 - P_f))]^{1/m}, with a comparison such as 0.25\sigma_0 at m = 5 against 0.71\sigma_0 at m = 20
Size effect \sigma \propto V^{-1/m} (larger for low m), or bend strength above tensile strength
Limitations: several flaw populations, service conditions, slow crack growth; proof testing or SPT diagrams

6a.watch:
• m describes scatter, not the strength level: a material can have a high mean strength and a low m.
  • Survival P_s = 1 - P_f goes inside the double logarithm.

6b.fix: Slides 8 and 9 reproduce a bending-geometry figure whose four-point moment diagram is labelled PL/2. With loads P/2 applied a distance D from each support, the constant maximum moment is PD/2, which is less than the three-point value PL/4 because D < L/2. The slide's own four-point formula, \sigma = 3PD/(BW^2) = 6M/(BW^2), uses M = PD/2.
6b.html:
Given: nine 3-point bend MOR values from bars of one size: 178, 318, 345, 210, 296, 235, 248, 276, 262 MPa.

Find: (i) the Weibull modulus m; (ii) the median strength (P_f = 0.5); (iii) the normalised stress \sigma_0, the normalising parameter of the Weibull equation (the characteristic strength, P_f = 1 - 1/e = 0.632).

Step 1, Weibull form (slide 11).

P_f = 1 - \exp\left[-\left(\frac{\sigma}{\sigma_0}\right)^m\right] \quad\Rightarrow\quad \ln\ln\frac{1}{1 - P_f} = m\ln\sigma - m\ln\sigma_0

A plot of y = \ln\ln(1/P_s) against x = \ln\sigma is a straight line of slope m.

Step 2, rank the bars and give the j-th weakest P_f = j/(N + 1) with N = 9:

j\sigma (MPa)P_fx = \ln\sigmay = \ln\ln[1/(1 - P_f)]
11780.15.182-2.250
22100.25.347-1.500
32350.35.460-1.031
42480.45.513-0.672
52620.55.568-0.367
62760.65.620-0.087
72960.75.6900.186
83180.85.7620.476
93450.95.8440.834

Step 3, least-squares line.

\begin{aligned} \bar{x} &= 5.5541, \qquad \bar{y} = -0.4902 \\ S_{xx} &= \sum(x - \bar{x})^2 = 0.3422, \qquad S_{xy} = \sum(x - \bar{x})(y - \bar{y}) = 1.6276 \\ m &= \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}} = \frac{1.6276}{0.3422} = 4.76 \\ c &= \bar{y} - m\bar{x} = -0.4902 - 4.756 \times 5.5541 = -26.90 \end{aligned}

Step 4, normalised stress. At \sigma = \sigma_0 the line crosses y = 0:

\ln\sigma_0 = -\frac{c}{m} = \frac{26.90}{4.756} = 5.657 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \sigma_0 = 286\ \mathrm{MPa}

Step 5, median. At P_f = 0.5, (\sigma/\sigma_0)^m = \ln 2:

\sigma_{med} = \sigma_0(\ln 2)^{1/m} = 286.3 \times (0.6931)^{1/4.756} = 286.3 \times 0.926 = 265\ \mathrm{MPa}

The middle bar, 262 MPa, sits at P_f = 0.5 and agrees.

Answer: (i) m \approx 4.8; (ii) median strength \approx 265\ \mathrm{MPa}; (iii) normalised stress \sigma_0 \approx 286\ \mathrm{MPa}. An m below 5 means wide scatter: for 1 failure in 1000 bars, \sigma = \sigma_0(1.0005\times10^{-3})^{1/4.76} = 67\ \mathrm{MPa}, only a quarter of the median.
pts: Linearises the Weibull equation: \ln\ln[1/(1 - P_f)] = m\ln\sigma - m\ln\sigma_0
Ranks the data and assigns P_f = j/(N + 1) (or another stated estimator)
Correct table of \ln\sigma and double logarithms (for example -2.250 at 178 MPa and 0.834 at 345 MPa)
(i) Slope by least squares or a drawn best line: m \approx 4.8 (5.3 with (j - 0.3)/(N + 0.4), 5.9 with (j - 0.5)/N)
States that m \approx 5 means wide scatter and low reliability (a design stress far below the median)
Intercept c \approx -26.9 and \ln\sigma_0 = -c/m
(iii) \sigma_0 \approx 286\ \mathrm{MPa}, named as the normalising (characteristic) stress at P_f = 0.632
Median from P_f = 0.5: \sigma_{med} = \sigma_0(\ln 2)^{1/m}

6b.watch:
• "Normalised stress" is read here as \sigma_0, the parameter that makes \sigma/\sigma_0 dimensionless; some texts call it the normalising parameter. If your course notes define it differently, say which you use.
  • Put P_s = 1 - P_f inside the double logarithm. Using \ln\ln(1/P_f) gives a negative slope.
  • The estimator changes m slightly: (j - 0.3)/(N + 0.4) gives m = 5.3 and \sigma_0 = 285\ \mathrm{MPa}. Nine bars are far fewer than the 30 needed to fix m within about 20 %.
  • These are 3-point MOR values, which exceed the uniform-tension strength of the same material (smaller highly stressed volume, slide 9).

7a.html:
A ceramic breaks in tension from a flaw when K_I = Y\sigma\sqrt{\pi c} reaches K_{IC}, so \sigma_f = K_{IC}/(Y\sqrt{\pi c}). The worst flaws and, in bending, the highest tension are at the surface (slide 8). Pre-stressing lowers the tension those flaws feel; crack deflection raises the resistance K_{IC}.

Pre-stressing. A residual compression \sigma_r is locked into the surface, balanced by tension in the core. An applied tension must first cancel it:

K_I = Y(\sigma_a - \lvert\sigma_r\rvert)\sqrt{\pi c}, \qquad \sigma_{f,\text{apparent}} \approx \sigma_f + \lvert\sigma_r\rvert
  • Thermal tempering of glass: heat above T_g, near the softening point (about 620 to 650^\circ\mathrm{C} for soda-lime glass, T_g \approx 560^\circ\mathrm{C}), and blast with cold air. The surface stiffens first; the hot core contracts later and pulls it into compression. The profile is parabolic, surface compression about twice the core tension.
  • Ion exchange (chemical strengthening): larger \mathrm{K^+} replaces \mathrm{Na^+} below T_g; the crowded layer reaches several hundred MPa of compression.
  • Others: a glaze with lower expansion than the body, a shrink-fitted steel ring around a ceramic die, or grinding-induced t to m in zirconia surfaces.

The stored core tension sets a limit: a crack through the layer releases it, and tempered glass dices into small, blunt fragments.

Crack deflection (slide 12). Second-phase particles, platelets, whiskers, elongated grains (self-reinforced \mathrm{Si_3N_4}), weak grain boundaries or thermal-mismatch stresses tilt and twist the crack out of the plane normal to the stress.

  • The deflected tip is loaded in mixed mode: k_1 \approx \cos^3(\theta/2)K_I, about 0.79K_I for \theta = 45^\circ, so a higher applied stress is needed.
  • The tortuous path makes more fracture surface per unit advance and absorbs more energy.
  • The gain rises with volume fraction (to about 20 %) and aspect ratio: twisting around rods can about double K_{IC}, spheres give less.

Both raise strength for the same flaw: pre-stress by \lvert\sigma_r\rvert, deflection in proportion to K_{IC}.
pts: Sets the basis: tensile failure from surface flaws, \sigma_f = K_{IC}/(Y\sqrt{\pi c})
Pre-stress: residual surface compression balanced by core tension; K_I = Y(\sigma_a - \lvert\sigma_r\rvert)\sqrt{\pi c}, strength raised by \lvert\sigma_r\rvert
Thermal tempering mechanism: surface cools first, core contracts later; parabolic profile, surface compression about twice the core tension
Ion exchange (\mathrm{K^+} for \mathrm{Na^+}) or another method (glaze, shrink fit, surface t to m)
Limit: damage through the layer releases the core tension (dicing of tempered glass)
Crack deflection: particles, whiskers, elongated grains or weak interfaces tilt and twist the crack
Mixed-mode loading lowers the local K_I (\cos^3(\theta/2), about 0.79 at 45^\circ)
Longer path absorbs more energy; K_{IC} up to about twice, best with rods or platelets at about 20 vol%
Sketch of the stress profile and the deflected crack path
7a.sketch:
• Stress profile: compression at both surfaces, tension in the core, and the reduced net tension at the loaded surface.
  • Crack path: tilted and twisted around particles or elongated grains, compared with the straight path.
7a.src: Mechanical properties, slides 4, 6, 8, 12; Carter and Norton, Ceramic Materials, pp 350-351, 486, 488
7a.watch:
• Pre-stressing does not change K_{IC} or remove flaws; it only lowers the net surface tension, so it fails if service damage cuts deeper than the compressive layer.
  • Tempered glass cannot be cut or drilled afterwards; it is shaped first.
  • Some texts say "about 150^\circ\mathrm{C} above T_g". Soda-lime glass (T_g \approx 560^\circ\mathrm{C}, softening point about 730^\circ\mathrm{C}) is tempered from about 620 to 650^\circ\mathrm{C}; much hotter and the sheet sags.
